description: A comprehensive study guide covering the fundamental principles of gravitation, the behavior of acceleration due to gravity, planetary motion, and satellite dynamics, optimized for competitive exam preparation.

sections.title: Universal Law of Gravitation
sections.description: Fundamental concepts defining the attractive force between bodies in the universe and the acceleration experienced by free-falling objects.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2 (where G is the Universal Gravitational Constant)
scientific_principles.application: Used to calculate the attractive force between any two point masses in the universe, such as the Earth and the Moon.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: g = GM / R^2 (where M is mass of Earth and R is radius of Earth)
scientific_principles.application: Determines the acceleration of objects falling freely towards the surface of the Earth.

important_facts.fact: The Universal Gravitational Constant (G) is 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, which was first accurately measured by Henry Cavendish.
The standard value of 'g' on the surface of the Earth is taken as 9.8 m/s^2.

sections.title: Variation in Acceleration due to Gravity ('g')
sections.description: Factors causing the value of 'g' to change across different locations and conditions on or around the Earth.

key_concepts.explanation: Earth is not a perfect sphere; it is an oblate spheroid. Because the equatorial radius is greater than the polar radius, 'g' is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator.
The value of 'g' decreases when moving above the Earth's surface (altitude) and also when going deep below the surface (depth). The value of 'g' becomes zero at the exact center of the Earth.

The rotation of the Earth creates a centrifugal force that reduces the effective value of 'g' at the equator. If the Earth were to suddenly stop rotating, the value of 'g' at the equator would increase.

sections.title: Mass, Weight, and Apparent Weight in a Lift
sections.description: Distinctions between mass and weight, and the phenomena of weightlessness experienced in moving elevators.

key_concepts.explanation: Mass (m) is the amount of matter in a body and remains constant everywhere. Weight (W = mg) is a force dependent on gravity and varies depending on location.
When an elevator accelerates upwards with uniform acceleration, the apparent weight of a person standing inside increases (W' = m(g + a)).
When an elevator accelerates downwards with uniform acceleration, the apparent weight of a person decreases (W' = m(g - a)).
If the elevator cable breaks, it falls freely with acceleration 'g'. The apparent weight of the person becomes zero, a state known as weightlessness.

sections.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
sections.description: Three fundamental laws formulated by Johannes Kepler that describe the motion of planets around the Sun.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun situated at one of the focal points.
scientific_principles.application: Describes the non-circular trajectory of celestial bodies in the solar system.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: The line that connects a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. (Areal velocity is constant)
scientific_principles.application: Proves that a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun (perihelion) and slower when it is farther away (aphelion).

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: The square of the time period of revolution (T^2) of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (mean distance, r^3) of its orbit.
scientific_principles.application: Explains why planets located further from the Sun take significantly longer to complete one orbit.

sections.title: Satellites, Orbital Velocity, and Escape Velocity
sections.description: Types of artificial satellites and the critical velocities required for orbiting and escaping celestial bodies.

key_concepts.explanation: Satellites placed in an equatorial orbit at an altitude of approximately 36,000 km. They have a time period of 24 hours, appearing stationary relative to Earth. Mainly used for telecommunications.
Satellites that revolve in low Earth orbits (500-800 km) passing over the poles in a north-south direction. Primarily used for weather monitoring and remote sensing.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: v_o = sqrt(gR) (For a satellite orbiting very close to Earth's surface)
scientific_principles.application: The minimum velocity required to put a satellite into its stable orbit around a planet.
The minimum velocity required for an object to completely overcome Earth's gravitational pull and never fall back.

important_facts.fact: The escape velocity for Earth is approximately 11.2 km/s.
The escape velocity for the Moon is only 2.38 km/s, which is why gas molecules escape easily, leaving the Moon without an atmosphere.
